objectives: Explain how a sliding-window rate rule decides when to alert
Plan a sequence of Modbus writes that stays below documented IDS thresholds
Propose detections that low-and-slow traffic cannot avoid
takeaways: A rate rule counts events inside a sliding window and alerts only when the count reaches a threshold.
Events leave the window as time passes, so slow, patient traffic never builds up a count.
The CybICS Modbus rules look only at the function code, not at the register or the value written.
Any noisy side activity, such as a port scan, can trigger a different rule and spoil an otherwise quiet attack.
Allow-lists, long-term baselines and firewalls catch or stop traffic that rate rules miss.

checkpoints.question: A rule fires at 10 writes in 30 seconds. You sent 4 writes, then waited 40 seconds. How many of them still count?
checkpoints.explanation: After 40 seconds all four writes have aged out of the 30-second window, so the count is back to zero. 4 assumes the rule remembers forever, but a sliding window forgets on its own. The register does not matter; the rule only looks at the function code.

quiz.question: Which change would let the CybICS IDS catch a single write from the attack machine?
options: Alerting on any write from an unlisted host
Counting reads as well as writes per source
quiz.explanation: An allow-list rule has no threshold to stay under: the first write from an unexpected host alerts. Shortening the window sounds stricter but makes evasion easier, because writes age out sooner, and counting reads still needs a threshold the single write stays below.

quiz.question: During your evasion window you run a quick nmap scan of OpenPLC. What is the most likely result?
options: Nothing, nmap does not send any Modbus
port_scan fires and the attempt fails
Nothing, the check only counts writes
The scan is counted as a Modbus write
quiz.explanation: The check fails on any new alert since the window opened, not only Modbus alerts or writes. A scan touches many ports in a few seconds and trips port_scan, so the attempt is lost.

quiz.question: Which pieces of information does the CybICS Modbus write rule use? (Select all that apply)
quiz.explanation: The rule counts write function codes per source address over time. It never reads the value or the register, even though both sit in the same request, which is why a process-aware check is a useful addition.

quiz.question: True or false: a rate rule that stays silent during your low-and-slow attack is working exactly as designed.
quiz.explanation: True. The rule measures rate, and your rate was low, so silence is the designed result rather than a bug. Evasion exploits what a rule looks at; fixing it means adding checks that look at something else.

quiz.question: Why does a defender benefit from practising this attack?
options: To learn which thresholds are safe to raise further
To find the rules' blind spots and cover them
To tune the rules so evasion raises alerts
To prove the IDS can block slow attacks
quiz.explanation: Testing detection the way an attacker would shows which traffic slips through, so new checks such as allow-listing can cover it. Raising thresholds would widen the blind spot, and no tuning makes an IDS block anything.
